back: A cud-chewing animal with a four-compartment stomach (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum) whose microbes digest fibre: cattle, sheep, goats.
An animal with one simple stomach that does not chew the cud: pigs, poultry, rabbits, horses, donkeys.
A useful material obtained in addition to the main product, e.g. hides, bones, blood, feathers, horns, hooves, manure.

front: Why ruminants can live on grass
back: Microbes in the rumen ferment cellulose, which the animal cannot digest itself, so roughage is turned into meat and milk.

front: What do ruminants have instead of upper incisors?
back: A hard dental pad; the lower incisors cut grass against it.

front: Which non-ruminants ferment fibre in the caecum?

back: Food (meat, milk, eggs), income, draught power, manure, savings, cultural uses (bride wealth), use of dry land, raw materials (hides, wool).
Hides, bones (bone meal), blood (blood meal), horns, hooves, offal and dung.
